This is going to be a bit long but I thought I would keep this conversation going if anyone is interested in continuing this debate. Many people disagreed with my views and if I am wrong I would like to either know why or strengthen my own resolve in my views by pitting them against peoples objections. Please no 'devils advocate', only respond with disagreement if you truly disagree.

I recently got into a debate where I agreed with Scott Adams that free speech should be enforced by the government online. Now, I have a more narrow, less dramatic idea of how this should play out so I thought I would share it. Imo, web applications that hold a virtual monopoly on (specific niches) of social media should be forced, by the government, to respect freedom of speech within certain contexts depending on the type of media in question. This hypothetical law, ironically, would not include smaller competitors like voat or gab or whatever but only the people that are wielding a pseudo-natural-monopoly and it would not give the government the power to just shut down a website it doesn't like, it would just allow users to sue, and win a settlement if it's found to be true, the top web applications when they have been censored and have not done anything illegal and were not engaging in spam. I am open to changing my mind about this so if anyone has a counter argument I'm interested in hearing it. Here are some of my reasons for believing this and some of my counter arguments to arguments I have heard.

The first objection many people make to this is that any government involvement in "policing the internet" would lead to totalitarianism. My response to this is that the government already does this now and has been doing it for years. If a web application is found to be breaking the law, the government has the full authority to hold them accountable. Therefore, this idea that government enforced free speech would set the initial precedent for of government control over the internet is false. This just adds a new law that the government would have to enforce.

The second objection I've heard about this is that terms like "pseudo-natural monopoly", "virtual utility" and "virtual-monopoly" are vague terms and that the key players who would be affected by this would therefore be defined arbitrarily. The problem with this argument is that all concepts that are 'new' start out as being 'vague'. I imagine that the differentiation between shapes, such as a triangle and square was once vague in primitive societies but they were eventually sharply defined. The US border was once 'vaguely defined'. The differences between species were once 'vaguely defined', the sciences were once 'vaguely defined'. There is no reason that such a term and a concept, given whatever name, could not be sharply defined. So the case that it is 'arbitrarily defined' isn't a meaningful counter argument.

The third argument is that this is not a natural monopoly. I argue that it is a virtual or pseudo natural monopoly. It is true that many developers, junior developers even, can spin up a web application, a clone of reddit, of Facebook, or create a search engine and the barrier to entry in terms of raw technology is, in mosts cases, low. But this misses the bigger picture. The physical infrastructure is not all that is needed to produce the raw content of value. People primarily don't visit sites like Twitter, Facebook, and Google for the quality of the web applications, they visit it for the content. Users are the ones providing 'the content', which is the object of value that they visit these web applications for, and when users coagulate around one web application there is little need for a second that does exactly the same thing. Voat is not an exception. Although there is a community here it is microscopic compared to reddit. Virtually every sub at voat is a ghost town. It's not because it's an inferior web application, it's basically a clone of reddit, it's that people go where the content is, which is where people already are. The content itself is the people and the people are going there for the content, so in that sense the coagulative nature of the material, this recursive quirk of the web application market, makes it a pseudo-natural-monopoly. It is a complex concept to define but it is not impossible to define and the complexity of the concept does not make it erroneous.

The fourth objection I have heard is that bigger web applications, like facebook, twitter and google, will use the government to "shut down" competitors by making false claims about them not respecting free speech. But in my opinion, competitors who do not hold a virtual monopoly on social media niches would not be liable, so this argument only holds if the definition of a 'virtual-utility' or 'pseudo-natural-monopoly' is mutable, and I don't advocate that the term should be changeable willy nilly. And the argument that the definition of a law could be changed willy nilly into anything is an argument that could be extrapolated and used on any law, so it's not much of an argument.

The fifth objection is that this would force small businesses to comply with more government regulations. My response is that this wouldn't. It would only force a handful of exceptional web applications to comply with more government regulations.

The sixth objection is "how would the government regulate web apps that serve as virtual utilities serving content from overseas'? I would argue that they should be incentivized by way of taxation and perhaps stricter measures if necessary. An outright ban is not something the government should be doing but they should definitely promote free speech among web applications that are serving as virtual utlities.

The seventh objection is that creating alternative competitive web applications in the free market is a better idea than more government involvement. My response is based on what I wrote earlier. The value of the web applications is the users themselves, and by virtue of human nature. people tend to gel together on one platform to do one niche social behavior. An empirical proof of this, and a demonstration that this is not just a 'theory' is when google tried to compete with facebook for it's niche in social media. Google, the half-a-trillion-dollar company with thousands of employees, billions of users already signed up who google automatically signed up, tried twice to compete with Facebook and failed twice. If a company as powerful as google can not compete for a niche in social media we can safely say that the barrier to entry for competition is high enough to constitute a pseudo-natural-monopoly.

Finally, not a counter argument, but I think the possible benefits outweigh the costs. If you just lay it out on a scale, on one hand you have billions of people being able to have free speech online on the most used web applications and all the enlightenment that will be spread as a result versus tremendous hundred billion dollar companies having the 'freedom' to censor it's users for their political views, I have to say that in my opinion even if there are costs to a measure like this, the benefits would be much higher.

We tolerate government involvement in private businesses for a hundred million thing, they are involved in a mind boggling number of ways that effect us negatively, this would be one of the only things that would almost certainly have positive repercussions and it seems a bit dumb to object to it imo. Or at least, a government rule forcing people to respect free speech in places that operate almost as if they were the public square should be the last thing one should object to if they believe government involvement leads to corruption. That's just my opinion.
